title: Stasimon 1 (lines 695–739)

teacherSummary.text: The elders praise Colonus and Athens: the nightingale, the river Cephisus, Athena's olive, and Poseidon's gifts of the horse and the oar.

vocabulary.definition: never cut back or trimmed by a gardener
vocabulary.context:
And here there grows, unpruned, untamed,
Terror to foemen’s spear,
A tree in Asian soil unnamed,
By Pelops’ Dorian isle unclaimed,
Self-nurtured year by year;
’Tis the grey-leaved olive that feeds our boys;
Nor youth nor withering age destroys
The plant that the Olive Planter tends
And the Grey-eyed Goddess herself defends.
vocabulary.source: Liber et Libri contextual definition, hand-written against the line in Oedipus at Colonus (Sappho unit, 2026-10-22)

segments.script: First, meaning. I read “Thou hast come to a steed-famed land for rest, / O stranger worn with toil, / To a land of all lands the goodliest / Colonus’ glistening soil.” slowly and put it in my own words: The elders tell the weary stranger that he has come to rest in a land famous for horses, the best land of all, the shining soil of Colonus. Next, craft. I notice the song piles up praise words, steed-famed, goodliest, glistening, as if welcoming a guest. The strongest word is “rest”: the thing Oedipus has sought since Apollo's promise. Then, effect. Why does the ode promise rest to a stranger the elders first tried to drive away? My answer: The ode promises rest to the stranger because the elders now receive Oedipus as a guest under Theseus' protection; the praise of Colonus turns the place of his exile into a home.
